176.title: Harden not your hearts (Psalm 94 [95])
176.hook: the psalm that opens the Church's daily prayer: today if you shall hear his voice
176.tomorrow: Bless the Lord, O my soul (Psalm 102 [103])
176.howItsDone: Catholics who pray the Liturgy of the Hours begin each day with the Invitatory: 'Lord, open my lips' with a small sign of the cross on the lips, then an antiphon and usually Psalm 94 [95], before the first hour of the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a guardian angel, and a psalm the devil quoted. Your line was under his wings. Did you pause at the door? A new week, and the psalm that most often opens the day. Day one hundred seventy-six.

Every morning, in monasteries, convents, rectories and a lot of ordinary kitchens, the first words of the Church's daily prayer are the same. Before any psalm, before any reading, someone traces a small cross on their lips and says: Lord, open my lips, and my mouth will declare your praise. It's a line from the Miserere, the psalm from five days ago. And then, right away, comes a psalm, on most days the same one. It's the doorbell of the whole day's prayer.
screen: `A CROSS TRACED ON THE LIPS.` → `LORD, OPEN MY LIPS.` → `THE DOORBELL OF THE DAY.`

segments.voice: That opening is called the Invitatory, from the Latin for invitation. Its usual psalm is Psalm 94 in the Douay, 95 in most Bibles, and it begins exactly like an invitation: "Come let us praise the Lord with joy: let us joyfully sing to God our saviour." Come. Let's go. It's plural; nobody's praying alone. It moves through God as maker of the deep places of the earth and the mountain peaks, the sea and the dry land. Then it slows down: "Come let us adore and fall down: and weep before the Lord that made us. For he is the Lord our God: and we are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand." And then, suddenly, the tone changes completely: "To day if you shall hear his voice, harden not your hearts." Then God himself speaks, and reminds them of the desert, when their ancestors, thirsty and angry, tested God at a place called Massah and Meribah, testing and quarreling, even though they'd seen everything he'd done. They heard, and their hearts went hard. It's a warning tucked inside an invitation. The Letter to the Hebrews picks up that one word, today, and presses on it: encourage one another every day, as long as it's still called today. Every morning, the Church hears it fresh. Not yesterday. Not some better tomorrow. Today. And the practical question it asks is simple: if God spoke to you today, in a person, a moment, a line you read, would you be soft enough to notice?
screen: `INVITATORY: AN INVITATION.` · `COME, LET US PRAISE.` · `TO DAY IF YOU SHALL HEAR HIS VOICE.` · `NOT YESTERDAY, NOT TOMORROW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen for one minute before praying. Settle, and breathe. Before saying anything, to God or to yourself, just listen. The room. The traffic. Your own breathing. The small voice in you that says the thing you've been avoiding. Don't answer it yet. Just hear it. Then, if you pray, you can trace a small cross on your lips and say, Lord, open my lips. If you don't, simply notice what you heard when you stopped talking. The bell holds the time.
Invitatory. The invitation that opens the Church's daily prayer, with the psalm that says: today, if you hear his voice. Today's word.
Your line: today, if you hear. Today, when someone tells you something you'd rather not hear, let it in before you answer. Day one hundred seventy-six.

177.title: Bless the Lord, O my soul (Psalm 102 [103])
177.hook: he knows we are dust, and his mercy is from eternity
177.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 102 [103] in the Liturgy of the Hours and hear it often at Mass as a responsorial psalm of mercy, with the refrain drawn from its line that the Lord is kind and merciful.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Invitatory, the psalm that opens every day of the Church's prayer. Your line was today, if you hear. What did you let in? Today, a psalm that talks to itself. Day one hundred seventy-seven.

Have you ever talked to yourself out loud? Come on. You can do this. Don't forget your keys. Most people do it, usually under their breath, usually in the car or the kitchen. It's how you get your own attention. The psalms do it too. Several times the one praying stops talking to God and turns to talk to their own soul, like giving yourself a nudge. And one psalm does nothing else in its opening lines. It's a pep talk to the self, and the subject is gratitude.
screen: `COME ON. YOU CAN DO THIS.` → `TALKING TO YOUR OWN SOUL.` → `A PEP TALK FOR GRATITUDE.`

segments.voice: Psalm 102 in the Douay, 103 in most Bibles: "Bless the Lord, O my soul: and let all that is within me bless his holy name. Bless the Lord, O my soul, and never forget all he hath done for thee." The Hebrew word for soul here, nephesh, doesn't mean a ghostly inner part. It means your whole living self, even your throat, your breath. So: all of me, wake up and remember. Why does the soul need reminding? Because we forget good things fast. The psalm makes a list: he forgives, he heals, he redeems your life from destruction, he crowns you with mercy, he renews your youth like an eagle's. Then it says the most tender things about God in the whole psalter. "As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our iniquities from us." East and west never meet; you can walk forever and never reach where your sins went. "As a father hath compassion on his children, so hath the Lord compassion on them that fear him: for he knoweth our frame. He remembereth that we are dust." He remembers we're dust. Not to shame us, but to go easy on us. Then our shortness again, like the psalm of Moses: "Man's days are as grass." A wind passes over the flower and it's gone. "But the mercy of the Lord is from eternity and unto eternity upon them that fear him." The flower is short. The mercy isn't. And at the very end, the psalm turns outward: angels, heavenly hosts, all his works everywhere, bless the Lord. Then it comes home to where it began: bless the Lord, O my soul.
screen: `NEPHESH: YOUR WHOLE LIVING SELF.` · `AS FAR AS THE EAST FROM THE WEST.` · `HE REMEMBERETH THAT WE ARE DUST.` · `THE FLOWER IS SHORT, MERCY ISN'T.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name three good things. Settle, and breathe. Talk to yourself a little, the way the psalm does: come on, soul, remember. Then find three good things from the past few days. Not big ones. A meal, a text from a friend, a moment of sun, a thing that didn't go wrong. Name each one slowly and stay with it for a few breaths. If you pray, you can thank God for each: bless the Lord, O my soul. If you don't, let each one land fully before moving on. The bell holds the time.
Bless the Lord. The psalm's call to your whole self to remember, and to thank God, who knows we are dust. Today's word.
Your line: forget not his benefits. Tonight, before sleep, name the three good things again, and add one more from today. Day one hundred seventy-seven.

178.title: All creation (Psalm 103 [104])
178.hook: springs, cedars, wild goats, the sea full of creatures
178.howItsDone: Catholics sing Psalm 103 [104] as the responsorial psalm at Pentecost, with its line about sending forth the Spirit to renew the face of the earth, and at the Easter Vigil after the creation reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bless the Lord, a psalm talking to its own soul. Your line was forget not his benefits. What good thing did you add last night? Today, the very next psalm, and it starts the same way. Day one hundred seventy-eight.

Put on a nature documentary. Mountain goats balanced on a cliff that looks impossible. A whale surfacing, enormous and unhurried. Lions at dusk. A spring bubbling out of a rock, and birds lining up to drink. The narrator's voice goes quiet with wonder. Long before cameras, someone made the same film in words. It's a psalm that walks through the whole created world, one creature at a time, and it plays like a nature documentary.
screen: `GOATS ON A CLIFF.` → `A WHALE SURFACING.` → `A DOCUMENTARY IN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Psalm 103 in the Douay, 104 in most Bibles, opens with the same line as the psalm before it: bless the Lord, O my soul. But this time the reason isn't mercy. It's the world. God is clothed with light as with a garment, stretching out the sky like a tent. Then the tour begins. Springs run down between the hills, and wild asses come to drink. Birds nest by the water and sing among the branches. Grass for the cattle, and for people, the psalm lists three gifts: "wine may cheer the heart of man," oil to make the face shine, and bread to strengthen the heart. The cedars of Lebanon, planted by God, with sparrows nesting there and the heron's house in the highest of them. And then a line the Douay makes delightful: "The highest mountains are a refuge for the harts, the rock for the irchins." Irchins are hedgehogs. The Hebrew seems to mean a small rock animal, the hyrax, but the Latin chose hedgehogs, and so the Douay gave God's rocks to the hedgehogs. The moon marks the seasons, lions roar for their prey at night, and people go out to work until evening. Then the sea, with creatures without number, ships sailing across it, and the great sea creature God made "to play therein." In the Douay, the sea dragon is made to play. And at the summit: "How great are thy works, O Lord? thou hast made all things in wisdom." Everything waits on God for food; when God takes away their breath, they die. And then the line the Church sings at Pentecost: "Thou shalt send forth thy spirit, and they shall be created: and thou shalt renew the face of the earth."
screen: `CLOTHED WITH LIGHT.` · `WINE, OIL AND BREAD.` · `THE ROCK FOR THE IRCHINS.` · `A SEA CREATURE MADE TO PLAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go outside and name what you see. If you can, step out now, or later today. If you can't, look out a window. Settle, and breathe. Then, like the psalm, make a slow list. A tree. A bird. A cloud. A dog walking its person. Weeds in a crack in the sidewalk. Name each one quietly, and give it a breath before the next. If you pray, you can end with the psalm's line: how great are thy works, O Lord. If you don't, let the list be its own kind of wonder. The bell holds the time.
All creation. The psalm's tour of the world, from springs and cedars to hedgehogs and the sea, all made in wisdom. Today's word.
Your line: how great are thy works. Today, stop for one living thing you'd normally walk past, and look at it for ten full seconds. Day one hundred seventy-eight.

179.title: The Sunday evening psalm (Psalm 109 [110])
179.hook: the psalm that opens Sunday Vespers, about a priest forever like Melchisedech
179.tomorrow: From the rising of the sun (Psalm 112 [113])
179.howItsDone: Catholics who pray the Liturgy of the Hours say Vespers (Evening Prayer) at the end of the day, and on every Sunday it opens with Psalm 109 [110]; in cathedrals and monasteries it is often sung, sometimes with incense.

segments.voice: Yesterday, all creation, from springs and cedars to hedgehogs on the rocks. Your line was how great are thy works. What living thing did you stop for? Today, an evening psalm. Day one hundred seventy-nine.

Sunday, late afternoon. The light is going gold. In a monastery somewhere, a bell rings, and the monks file into their stalls facing each other across the choir. Somewhere else, a handful of people gather in a cathedral side chapel. In a city apartment, someone opens an app. They're all about to pray the same thing at the same hour, the Church's evening prayer. And on every Sunday, week after week, it begins with the same psalm, a psalm about a king and a very mysterious priest.
screen: `SUNDAY, THE LIGHT GOING GOLD.` → `A BELL, AND THE MONKS FILE IN.` → `THE SAME PSALM EVERY SUNDAY.`

segments.voice: The evening prayer is called Vespers, from the Latin vesper, evening, the same word for the evening star. It's one of the two great hinges of the Church's daily prayer, with Lauds in the morning. It gathers up the day and offers it back, often with incense rising and a candle lit. And Sunday Vespers opens with Psalm 109 in the Douay, 110 in most Bibles: "The Lord said to my Lord: Sit thou at my right hand: Until I make thy enemies thy footstool." It's a royal psalm, a king being enthroned. Jesus himself puzzled his listeners with it. Matthew says he asked them, "What think you of Christ? whose son is he?" David's, they said. Then, he asked, how can David call him my Lord? "If David then call him Lord, how is he his son?" And no one could answer him a word. The New Testament comes back to this psalm again and again, hearing in it the risen Christ seated at God's right hand. Then comes the strangest line: "The Lord hath sworn, and he will not repent: Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech." Melchisedech appears in Genesis for just a few verses: a king of Salem who comes out to meet Abraham, "bringing forth bread and wine, for he was the priest of the most high God," and blesses him. Genesis gives him no family tree, and the Letter to the Hebrews makes much of that, calling him without beginning of days or end of life, and builds its picture of Christ's priesthood on him. Catholics still hear his name in the Roman Canon, the first Eucharistic Prayer, and this psalm can be sung when priests are ordained: a priest for ever.
screen: `VESPERS: THE EVENING PRAYER.` · `SIT THOU AT MY RIGHT HAND.` · `HOW IS HE HIS SON?` · `A PRIEST LIKE MELCHISEDECH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray at sunset. Today, when the light starts to go, stop for two minutes wherever you are. For now, settle and breathe, and imagine that moment. Look back over the day as the light fades: what it held, what it cost, what you'd hand back. If you pray, you can offer the day to God, the way Vespers does, perhaps with a line from any psalm you've learned. If you don't, simply watch the light change, and let the day end. The bell holds the time.
Vespers. The Church's evening prayer, which on Sundays opens with the psalm of a king and a priest for ever. Today's word.
Your line: a priest for ever. Tonight at sunset, stop, look west for one minute, and offer the day back. Day one hundred seventy-nine.

180.title: From the rising of the sun (Psalm 112 [113])
180.hook: God stoops down to lift the poor from the dust
180.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 112 [113] at Evening Prayer on some Sundays and on feasts, and hear it at Mass; in Latin it is known as Laudate pueri, and composers have set it for Vespers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vespers, and a priest for ever like Melchisedech. Your line was a priest for ever. Did you stop at sunset? Today, a psalm that runs from sunrise to sunset. Day one hundred eighty.

Right now, somewhere on earth, the sun is rising. Somewhere else it's setting. It's always coming up on someone's morning. Which means that at every single moment, someone somewhere is waking up, and someone is going to bed. A short psalm takes that fact and turns it into praise that never stops, a relay around the planet. And then, halfway through, it looks down from the sky, all the way down to the garbage heap at the edge of town.
screen: `ALWAYS SOMEONE'S SUNRISE.` → `PRAISE THAT NEVER STOPS.` → `DOWN TO THE GARBAGE HEAP.`

segments.voice: Psalm 112 in the Douay, 113 in most Bibles. It opens: "Praise the Lord, ye children: praise ye the name of the Lord." Children here follows the Latin, pueri, a word that can also mean servants, and the Hebrew does say servants: you who serve the Lord. Then the sun: "From the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same, the name of the Lord is worthy of praise." East to west, morning to night. Then it climbs as high as it can go. God is high above all nations, his glory above the heavens. Who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high? And then the great surprise. This God looks down, on the low things in heaven and in earth. And the psalm keeps going down: "Raising up the needy from the earth, and lifting up the poor out of the dunghill: That he may place him with princes, with the princes of his people." The dunghill was probably the town refuse heap, often explained as the place where the poorest people slept and begged. The God above the heavens stoops all the way down to the dump and seats someone from there at the royal table. Then one more: the barren woman is given a home, the joyful mother of children. Hannah sings nearly the same lines about the poor and the dunghill when her son is born, and Mary sings the same turning-over of the world in the Magnificat. This psalm begins the Hallel, the psalms of praise sung at Passover. Some readers think these were the hymn Jesus and his friends sang at the Last Supper before going out to the Mount of Olives.
screen: `YE CHILDREN, YE SERVANTS.` · `FROM SUNRISE TO SUNSET.` · `OUT OF THE DUNGHILL, TO PRINCES.` · `HANNAH, MARY, THE HALLEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: lift someone's spirits today. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who's low right now: discouraged, overlooked, stuck, sitting on their own small dunghill. Picture them. Now think of one small thing that might lift them a little: a message, a call, a compliment that's true, a coffee, an invitation to sit at your table. If you pray, you can pray for them in the psalm's words: raising up the needy. If you don't, simply hold them in mind, and decide on your one small thing. The bell holds the time.
Laudate pueri. Latin for praise, O servants, the psalm's name at Vespers, praise running around the world all day, to the God who stoops to lift the poor. Today's word.
Your line: he raises the needy. Today, do the one small thing you chose for that person, before the sun goes down. Day one hundred eighty.

181.title: The shortest psalm (Psalm 116 [117])
181.hook: two verses: praise the Lord, all nations
181.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 116 [117] in the Liturgy of the Hours, and it is often sung in Latin as Laudate Dominum; some pray it through the day as a short prayer of praise.

segments.voice: Yesterday, from the rising of the sun, Laudate pueri: the God who stoops down to lift the poor out of the dust. Your line was he raises the needy. Whose spirits did you lift? Day one hundred eighty-one.

Some psalms go on for pages. Some take ten minutes to pray. And then there's this one. You could say it while the kettle boils. You could say it in the time it takes a traffic light to change. Two verses. Under thirty words in the Douay. It's the shortest psalm in the Psalter. And yet in those few words it manages to invite the whole planet. Not one people, not one city, not one church. Everyone. Today: the shortest psalm.
screen: `SOME PSALMS RUN FOR PAGES.` → `THIS ONE: TWO VERSES.` → `AND IT INVITES EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Here is the whole thing, in the Douay-Rheims: "O praise the Lord, all ye nations: praise him, all ye people. For his mercy is confirmed upon us: and the truth of the Lord remaineth for ever." That's it. That's the psalm. First, the shape. The first verse is the invitation, and it's as wide as it can be: all nations, all peoples. The second verse gives the reason, and it's two old Hebrew words that run all through the Psalms. Mercy is chesed, the steady, loyal love that keeps a promise. Truth is emet, faithfulness, the thing you can lean your weight on. So the reason the whole world is invited to praise is simple: God's love holds, and God's faithfulness lasts. Second, where it sits. Like yesterday's psalm, it belongs to the Hallel, the psalms of praise sung at Passover and the great feasts, and it is still sung in Jewish worship today. Third, who picked it up. Saint Paul quotes this psalm in his letter to the Romans, to say the good news was meant for the nations, not one people alone. And the Church kept singing it in Latin, Laudate Dominum, omnes gentes. Mozart set it to music. Pilgrims at Taizé sing it over and over. So the shortest psalm travels far. A Catholic can pray it at Vespers, a Jewish family sings it at Passover, and both are singing the same two verses about everyone.
screen: `TWO VERSES: THE INVITE AND THE REASON.` · `MERCY AND TRUTH: LOVE THAT HOLDS.` · `SUNG AT PASSOVER, THEN AND NOW.` · `PAUL, MOZART, TAIZÉ: ALL NATIONS.` · then, large: `O PRAISE THE LORD, ALL YE NATIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the shortest psalm, three times. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, say the two verses slowly, once. Then again, and this time picture one place far from you, a country you've never visited, people waking up there right now. Then a third time, and picture someone near you who is nothing like you. If you don't pray, just hold those three pictures in the quiet: here, far away, and next door. The bell holds the time.
Laudate Dominum. Latin for praise the Lord, the shortest psalm in the whole Psalter: two verses that invite all nations. Today's word.
Your line: all nations. Today, when you see a face or hear an accent from somewhere far away, remember the psalm had room for them before you ever met them. Day one hundred eighty-one.

182.title: The alphabet psalm (Psalm 118 [119])
182.hook: 176 verses in 22 stanzas, one for each Hebrew letter, all about God's word
182.howItsDone: Catholics pray portions of Psalm 118 [119] in the Liturgy of the Hours, especially at the midday hours, usually one stanza at a time, and some read one stanza a day as lectio divina.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shortest psalm, Laudate Dominum: two verses for the whole world. Your line was all nations. Did someone from far away cross your path? Today, the longest. Day one hundred eighty-two.

Maybe you learned the alphabet with a song. A is for apple, B is for ball, all the way down to Z. Children love it because it has an order, and you always know where you are and how far is left. Now imagine someone doing that with a prayer. Taking every letter of their alphabet, in order, and writing eight lines for each one. Twenty-two letters. A hundred seventy-six verses. The longest psalm in the Bible, and the longest chapter too. Today: the alphabet psalm.
screen: `A IS FOR APPLE.` → `EIGHT LINES FOR EVERY LETTER.` → `THE LONGEST PSALM OF ALL.`

segments.voice: First, the shape. In Hebrew, this psalm is an acrostic. It has twenty-two stanzas, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, from aleph to tav. Every one of the eight lines in the first stanza begins with aleph. Every line in the second begins with beth. And so on to the end. Open a Douay-Rheims and you'll still see the letters printed as little headings: ALEPH, BETH, GHIMEL. English can't keep the trick, but it keeps the signposts. Second, the subject. The whole psalm, all hundred seventy-six verses, is about one thing: God's word. The poet keeps finding new names for it: law, testimonies, ways, precepts, commandments, justifications, words. Nearly every verse has one. It opens like this: "Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord." Third, the feeling. You might expect a psalm about law to sound like a rulebook. It doesn't. It sounds like a love letter. Halfway through, the poet says: "O how have I loved thy law, O Lord! it is my meditation all the day." For the psalmist, God's law isn't a fence. It's a gift, the way God has shown himself. Why an alphabet? Nobody knows for certain. Some say it helped people memorize it. Some say it's a way of saying everything, from A to Z, the whole of life, belongs to this love. Jews pray it, and so do Catholics: for centuries monks and priests prayed pieces of it every single day in the Divine Office, a stanza or two at a time.
screen: `TWENTY-TWO STANZAS, ALEPH TO TAV.` · `ONE SUBJECT: GOD'S WORD.` · `NOT A RULEBOOK. A LOVE LETTER.` · `EVERYTHING, FROM A TO Z.` · then, large: `O HOW HAVE I LOVED THY LAW, O LORD!`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one stanza. Settle, and breathe. If you have a Bible nearby, open to this psalm and read the first eight verses, the aleph stanza, slowly, out loud or in your head. If you don't, simply repeat the line we heard: blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. Notice which word catches you, and stay with that one. The bell holds the time.
Aleph. The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, opening the first stanza of the longest psalm: twenty-two stanzas, one for each letter, all about God's word. Today's word.

Your line: a to z of love. This week ran from the invitatory, through bless the Lord, all creation, Vespers, and the God who raises the needy, to the shortest psalm and the longest. Today, notice one ordinary thing, from alarm clock to lights out, that could belong to that love. Day one hundred eighty-two.

fork.setup: you're the psalmist writing a hundred seventy-six verses about God's word. how do you keep it from repeating one dull term?
options: use the word law every time.
keep finding new names: testimonies, ways, precepts, words.
stop after one stanza.
fork.reveal: the poet keeps finding new names for God's word, and nearly every verse holds one of them.

original.note: Hebrew: aleph, the first letter, which opens all eight lines of the first stanza.

trapdoor: what you thought: a very long psalm about rules.
what it means: a love poem about God's word, walked from the first letter to the last.
what a scholar hears: a strict acrostic, 22 × 8 lines, with a set of near-synonyms for torah threaded through almost every verse.
